name: Data scientist
summary: Data scientist interviews usually test statistics, machine learning, SQL and Python, then how you'd use them on a business problem: choosing a metric, designing an experiment, or building a model and explaining its limits. Candidates commonly report a take-home or case study and a deep dive into a past project, and for product-focused roles, questions on A/B testing.
rounds: Online test or technical screen: SQL, Python and statistics
Take-home or live case: analyse data or build a simple model, then present it (often)
Machine learning and statistics interview, often built around your own projects
Product or business case on metrics and experiments (for product-focused roles)
looks_for: Statistics you can explain: distributions, hypothesis tests, confidence intervals
Choosing a model and a metric that fit the problem, not the fashion
Careful validation: proper splits, overfitting, no information from the future in training data
SQL and Python for getting and cleaning data
Turning a vague business question into something you can test
Explaining results and uncertainty to people who aren't technical

questions.text: Tell me about a model or analysis of yours that was used to make a decision.
covers: The problem, the decision and who made it
Your approach and why you chose it over the alternatives
The impact, with a number, and how you checked it

questions.text: Describe a project where the data turned out much messier than you expected.
covers: What was wrong: missing values, a biased sample, definitions that changed over time
How you found it and what you did about it
How it changed your conclusions or your timeline

questions.text: Tell me about a time a model did worse once it was in use than it had in testing.
covers: The gap between offline and live results
The cause: drift, mismatched data, or features that weren't available at prediction time
What you changed in how you validate models

questions.text: Tell me about a time you chose a simpler approach over a more sophisticated one.
covers: Both options and what each would have cost
Why simple was good enough: accuracy, explainability, time to deliver
How it worked out

questions.text: Explain the bias-variance trade-off, and how you'd spot overfitting.
covers: Too simple a model misses patterns; too complex a model learns noise
Spotting it by comparing training and validation scores, or with learning curves
Fixes: more data, regularisation, a simpler model, cross-validation

questions.text: You're building a fraud detection model and only a tiny share of transactions are fraud. How do you evaluate it?
covers: Why accuracy misleads when one class is rare
Precision, recall and precision-recall curves, and choosing a threshold from the cost of each error
Class weights or resampling, and testing on data with the real fraud rate

questions.text: How would you design an A/B test for a new recommendation feature?
covers: A hypothesis, one main metric and a few guardrail metrics
What gets randomised (users, sessions), the sample size and how long to run it
Reading the result: significance, practical size of the effect, novelty effects

questions.text: Explain a confidence interval to a product manager.
covers: A range of plausible values for the thing being estimated
Why a wider range means less certainty, and what narrows it
A plain example from a test result

questions.text: What's the difference between correlation and causation, and how could you get closer to a causal answer without an experiment?
covers: Confounders and reverse causation, with an example
Natural experiments, matching, or a before-and-after comparison with a control group
Being clear about what the analysis can't prove

questions.text: How would you predict which customers are likely to cancel their subscription next month?
covers: Defining cancellation and the prediction window precisely
Features from usage, payments and support, built only from data before the prediction date
A simple baseline first, the evaluation metric, and how the business would act on the scores

questions.text: Compare logistic regression, random forests and gradient boosting. When would you pick each?
covers: Interpretability versus accuracy on tabular data
Training time, tuning effort and sensitivity to noisy data
What you'd try first and why

questions.text: How do you handle missing values, and when can that choice change your results?
covers: Why the data is missing: at random, or for a reason that matters
Dropping rows, simple filling, model-based filling, or adding a 'was missing' flag
Checking how sensitive the results are to the choice

questions.text: How would you use SQL to find each customer's first order, and whether they ordered again within 30 days? Talk me through it.
covers: Finding the first order per customer with MIN or a window function
Finding the next order with LEAD or a join back to the orders table
Handling customers with one order, and two orders on the same day

questions.text: How would you explain to a business team why the model made a particular prediction?
covers: Overall feature importance versus the reasons for one prediction
Tools such as SHAP values or partial dependence plots, in plain words
The limit: a feature being important doesn't make it a cause

questions.text: Your model's performance has been slowly dropping since launch. What could be happening, and what would you do?
covers: Data drift, changes in what the target means, or changes in upstream data
Monitoring input distributions and live performance once labels arrive
When to retrain on fresh data and when to rethink the model

questions.text: Why data science? How did you get into it?
covers: What got you started, and a project that hooked you
What you enjoy most: modelling, experiments, the business problem
What you're working to learn next

questions.text: What kinds of problems would you want to work on here as a data scientist?
covers: A grasp of the business and where data can help it
One or two specific problems you'd find interesting
How you'd measure success on them

tips: Know two projects inside out: the data, the baseline, the metric, what failed and what you'd do next.
Say what a simple baseline would score before you mention any complex model.
Practise explaining one statistical idea (p-values, confidence intervals, overfitting) in two sentences without jargon.
In case questions, ask how the result will be used; it decides the metric and the threshold.
Expect to write SQL and Python while talking; many screens test them before any machine learning.
